In this lab, you will construct a *sampling distribution* of a
statistic. Recall from class that the **sampling distribution of a
statistic** is the distribution of the statistic calculated from many
samples. It allows us to quantify and understand the sampling
variability (and more generally, the distribution) of a statistic. The
sampling distribution of a statistic is necessary for making both types
of inference (hypothesis tests and confidence intervals). In practice,
we usually work with a *model* for the sampling distribution. But in
this lab, we have the luxury of creating the population *and* having
access to resources (i.e. computing power) to take *many* samples from
this population, thereby constructing the actual sampling distribution.

::: {#boxedtext}
**Setting a seed:** We will take some random samples and build sampling
distributions in this lab, which means we should set a seed at the start
of your lab. This ensures reproducibility of your results, i.e. that you
get the same results every time you run the code.
<!---If this concept is new to you, review the lab on probability.--->
:::

```{r}
set.seed(1234)
```

## Getting Started

### Load packages

In this lab, we will explore and visualize the data using the
**tidyverse** suite of packages and the **openintro** package. We will
also use the **infer** package for resampling.

Let's load the packages. Again, if you're using the RStudio server, you
may not be able to load the **tidyverse** suite, and instead should load
the specific packages: **dplyr** and **ggplot2** as you've done in
previous labs. Modify the code below accordingly.

```{r load-packages, message=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(openintro)
library(infer)
```

### The data

A 2019 Gallup report states the following:

> The premise that scientific progress benefits people has been embodied
> in discoveries throughout the ages -- from the development of
> vaccinations to the explosion of technology in the past few decades,
> resulting in billions of supercomputers now resting in the hands and
> pockets of people worldwide. Still, not everyone around the world
> feels science benefits them personally.
>
> **Source:** [World Science Day: Is Knowledge
> Power?](https://news.gallup.com/opinion/gallup/268121/world-science-day-knowledge-power.aspx)

The Wellcome Global Monitor finds that 20% of people globally do not
believe that the work scientists do benefits people like them. In this
lab, you will assume this 20% is a true population proportion and learn
about how sample proportions can vary from sample to sample by taking
smaller samples from the population. We will first create our population
assuming a population size of 100,000. This means 20,000 (20%) of the
population think the work scientists do does not benefit them personally
and the remaining 80,000 think it does.

In the code below, we name our data frame `global_monitor` and the
variable that contains responses to the question *"Do you believe that
the work scientists do benefit people like you?"* `scientist_work`:

```{r}
global_monitor <- tibble(
  scientist_work = c(rep("Benefits", 80000), rep("Doesn't benefit", 20000))
)
```

We can visualize the distribution of these responses using a bar plot.

```{r bar-plot-pop, fig.height=2.5, fig.width=10}
global_monitor %>% ggplot(aes(x = scientist_work)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(
    x = "", y = "",
    title = "Do you believe that the work scientists 
    do benefit people like you?"
  ) +
  coord_flip() 
```

We can also obtain summary statistics to confirm we constructed the data
frame correctly.

```{r summ-stat-pop}
global_monitor %>%
  count(scientist_work) %>%
  mutate(p = n /sum(n))
```

## Sampling variability

<!---The unknown sampling distribution--->

In this lab, you have access to the entire population, but this is
rarely the case in real life. Gathering information on an entire
population is often extremely costly or impossible. Because of this, we
often take a sample of the population and use that to understand the
properties of the population.

If you are interested in estimating the proportion of people who don't
think the work scientists do benefits them, you can use the `sample_n`
command to take a sample of size $n$ people from the population.

```{r samp1}
samp1 <- global_monitor %>%
  sample_n(50)
```

This command takes a simple random sample of size 50 from the
`global_monitor` dataset, and assigns the result to `samp1`. This is
similar to randomly drawing names from a hat that contains the names of
all in the population. Working with these 50 names is considerably
simpler than working with all 100,000 people in the population.

1.  Describe the distribution of responses in this sample. How does it
    compare to the distribution of responses in the population?
    **Hint:** Although the `sample_n` function takes a random sample of
    observations (i.e. rows) from the dataset, you can still refer to
    the variables in the dataset with the same names. Code you presented
    earlier for visualizing and summarising the population data will
    still be useful for the sample, however be careful to not label your
    proportion `p` since you're now calculating a sample statistic, not
    a population parameter. You can customize the label of the
    statistics to indicate that it comes from the sample.

If you're interested in estimating the proportion of all people who do
not believe that the work scientists do benefits them, but you do not
have access to the population data, your best single guess is the sample
proportion.

Depending on which 50 people you selected, your estimate could be a bit
above or a bit below the true population proportion of 20%. In general,
though, the sample proportion turns out to be a pretty good estimate of
the true population proportion, and you were able to get it by sampling
less than 1% of the population.

2.  Would you expect the sample proportion to match the sample
    proportion of another student's sample? Why, or why not? If the
    answer is no, would you expect the proportions to be somewhat
    different or very different?

3.  Take a second sample, also of size 50, and call it `samp2`. How does
    the sample proportion of `samp2` compare with that of `samp1`?
    Suppose we took two more samples, one of size 100 and one of
    size 1000. Which would you think would provide a more accurate
    estimate of the population proportion?

Not surprisingly, every time you take another random sample, you might
get a different sample proportion. It's useful to get a sense of just
how much variability you should expect when estimating the population
proportion this way.

## Constructing a sampling distribution

The distribution of sample proportions, called the *sampling
distribution (of the proportion)*, can help you understand this
(sampling) variability. In this section, you''ll construct the sampling
distribution of the proportion of adults who do not believe the work of
scientists benefits people like them, based on samples of size $n=50$
adults.

In this lab, because you have access to the population and computing
power, you can construct the sampling distribution for the sample
proportion by actually taking samples from the population and repeating
that many times. In the code below, we ask R to take 15,000 different
samples of size 50 from the population, calculate the proportion of
responses in each sample, filter for only the *Doesn't benefit*
responses, and store each result in a vector called `sample_props50`.
The 15,000 different samples are known as *replicates*. The filter step
is so that we only keep the proportion who don't think science benefits
(we don't need to keep the proportion who *do* think science benefits).
We specify `replace = TRUE` since we want each person in the population
to have a 20% chance of not believing the work of scientists benefits
them.

```{r iterate}
sample_props50 <- global_monitor %>%
                    rep_sample_n(size = 50, reps = 15000, replace = TRUE) %>%
                    count(scientist_work) %>%
                    mutate(p_hat = n /sum(n)) %>%
                    filter(scientist_work == "Doesn't benefit")
```

And we can visualize the (sampling) distribution of these proportions
with a histogram:

```{r}
ggplot(data = sample_props50, aes(x = p_hat)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.02) +
  labs(
    x = "p_hat (Doesn't benefit)",
    title = "Sampling distribution of p_hat",
    subtitle = "Sample size = 50, Number of samples = 15000"
  )
```

1.  How many rows are there in `sample_props50`? What does each row
    represent? Describe the shape, center, and spread of this sampling
    distribution. Include the histogram of your distribution.

Note that in practice one rarely gets to build true sampling
distribution, because one rarely has access to the entire population.
Without the `rep_sample_n` function, this would be painful. We would
have to manually run the sampling 15,000 times! Note that for each of
the 15,000 times we computed a proportion, we did so from a *different*
sample.

## Effect of Sample Size on the Shape, Center, and Spread of a Sampling Distribution

1.  What would happen to the sampling distribution if we took a
    *smaller* or *larger* sample? In this section, we explore the effect
    of *sample size* on the shape, center, and spread of the sampling
    distribution of proportions of *Doesn't benefit*. So far, you've
    constructed a sampling distribution of proportions based on samples
    of size *50 adults*, using 15,000 replicates. Here you will
    construct sampling distributions of proportions based on samples of
    size $n=10$ and $n=100$ adults, still using 15,000 replicates.
    Review and understand your code from above where you constructed a
    sampling distribution of proportions based on $n=50$ adults, then
    modify it to construct sampling distributions based on samples of
    size $n=10$ and $n=100$ adults. Make a histogram of each of your
    sampling distributions.

<!-- -->

2.  For the two new sampling distributions you constructed (sample sizes
    10 and 100), answer the following questions: What does each
    observation in the sampling distribution represent? Describe the
    center (mean), spread (standard deviation, aka \`\`standard
    error''), and shape (symmetric/skewed) of the sampling distribution.
    How do these change as the sample size increases from 10 to 50 to
    100?

3.  Consider the sampling distribution where the sample size is 50. What
    do you think would happen to the shape and spread of the sampling
    distribution as you vary the number of replicates (aka Number of
    Samples) from 10 to infinity?

It turns out the sample proportion is what we call *unbiased*; this
means that the *center* of the sampling distribution is at the true
population proportion. Further, the spread of the distribution indicates
how much variability is incurred by sampling only 50 people at a time
from the population.
